---
title: "Installing R, RStudio, and Git"
subtitle: "Guide 1 of 4 · do this once"
---

You need three separate pieces of software. They are easy to confuse, so it is
worth being clear about what each one is:

| Software | What it is | Do you ever open it? |
|---|---|---|
| **R** | The language itself, plus the engine that runs your code | No, RStudio talks to it for you |
| **RStudio** | The editor you actually work in | Yes, this is the icon you click |
| **Git** | The version-control program that records your work | Rarely, RStudio drives it for you |

Install them in that order: R first, then RStudio, then Git.

## 1. Install R

Download it from [cloud.r-project.org](https://cloud.r-project.org/) and run the
installer with all the default options.

- **macOS:** choose the `.pkg` that matches your chip. Apple Silicon (M1 through
  M4) needs the **arm64** build; older Intel Macs need the **x86_64** build. If
  you pick the wrong one, R will still install but some packages will fail to
  load later.
- **Windows:** click "install R for the first time", then download the `.exe`.

## 2. Install RStudio

Download **RStudio Desktop** (the free open-source edition) from
[posit.co](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/) and install it with the
defaults.

Open RStudio once. It should find R by itself and print a banner in the Console
starting with `R version`, followed by whatever version you just installed. If
RStudio opens but the Console is
empty or complains that it cannot find R, R did not install correctly: reinstall
it and then restart RStudio.

Quarto, which turns your `.qmd` files into documents, ships inside RStudio. You
do not install it separately.

## 3. Install Git

::: {.panel-tabset}

### macOS

Open the **Terminal** tab in RStudio (bottom-left pane, next to Console) and run:

```bash
xcode-select --install
```

A system dialog appears. Click **Install** and wait a few minutes. This installs
Apple's command line developer tools, which include Git.

If it says `command line tools are already installed`, you already have Git and
you are done with this step.

### Windows

Download **Git for Windows** from [git-scm.com/download/win](https://git-scm.com/download/win)
and run the installer.

Accept every default. The defaults matter more than they look: they put `git` on
your system path, which is what lets RStudio find it. Do not change the editor or
path options unless you know why you are changing them.

After it finishes, **restart RStudio**. RStudio only looks for Git when it
starts, so a running RStudio will not notice the new installation.

### Linux

```bash
sudo apt install git      # Debian, Ubuntu
sudo dnf install git      # Fedora
```

:::

## 4. Check that it worked

In RStudio, click the **Terminal** tab (bottom-left pane, beside Console) and
type:

```bash
git --version
```

You want a version number back, such as `git version 2.39.5`. Any version is
fine; Git is stable and old versions work. If you get
`command not found`, see [Git is not installed or RStudio cannot find it](troubleshooting.qmd#git-not-found).

Then confirm RStudio itself knows where Git lives: **Tools > Global Options >
Git/SVN**. The "Git executable" box should hold a real path (`/usr/bin/git` on
macOS, something like `C:/Program Files/Git/bin/git.exe` on Windows) and
**Enable version control interface for RStudio projects** should be checked.

## 5. Install the R packages you will need

Paste this into the **Console** (the pane where R runs, not the Terminal) and
press Enter:

```r
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "usethis", "gitcreds"))
```

This takes several minutes the first time. Some output scrolls by in red; that is
normal progress reporting, not an error. What matters is whether the final lines
say the packages were unpacked and the prompt `>` comes back.

If you are asked *"Do you want to install from sources the package which needs
compilation?"*, answer `no` unless you have a reason to compile.

::: {.callout-tip}
## In this course

Add the course textbook package as well:

```r
install.packages("r02pro")
```

That gives you the `gm` and `sahp` datasets used throughout the exercises.
:::
